project.name: Assembly
project.tagline: A multi-agent software delivery orchestrator — built by an autonomous agent, one unattended run a day.
project.summary:
Assembly coordinates a team of specialized AI agents — architect, engineer, reviewer, tester — through a defined workflow to take a software task from issue to reviewed pull request. The interesting question it exists to answer is not whether one agent can write code, but whether a structured team of them produces measurably better software than a single agent given the same budget. Every design choice is aimed at making that comparison honest: fixed models, hidden tests, a frozen benchmark set, and a baseline single-agent arm to beat.

The project has a second, stranger property: Assembly is being built by an autonomous agent, running unattended once a day against a written operating contract. Nobody watches the run. It reads its own progress file, picks the next task, writes tests first, verifies green, commits, pushes, and rewrites its notes for the next run — which starts with no memory of this one.

technical_highlights.title: Spec-first, ~18k lines of it
technical_highlights.detail: The specification tree was written before the code and is the contract: module specs, interface definitions, milestones, and open questions. When a spec is ambiguous the agent files an open question rather than silently reinterpreting it.

technical_highlights.title: One authority for shared types
technical_highlights.detail: Every type crossing a module boundary is defined in interfaces.md and nowhere else — now 80 Pydantic models across §1–§11, split one file per artifact family with tests mirroring the source tree 1:1.

technical_highlights.title: Rules enforced where they are decidable
technical_highlights.detail: Spec rules become structure when possible (an approval's scope is a single-member Literal, so blanket approval is unrepresentable), a model_validator when decidable from one instance, and documentation when they need external context the type doesn't carry.

technical_highlights.title: Schemas that cannot drift
technical_highlights.detail: JSON Schema is exported from the models into a committed file, and CI regenerates and diffs it on every push — a type change without a re-export fails the build.

technical_highlights.title: Bounded, revertible increments
technical_highlights.detail: Each cycle is capped at 10 changed files and 400 lines, ships with tests, and cites the requirement ID it implements. Ten small green commits is a good run; one large one is a violation regardless of how much budget was left.

technical_highlights.title: Safe to abandon at any moment
technical_highlights.detail: Budget exhaustion is abrupt and can land mid-sentence, so every cycle ends with a checkpoint — green, commit, push, rewrite the progress file, push again. Worst case, one cycle's work is lost and the next run picks up cleanly.

status.verification: pytest 99 passed · ruff clean · mypy strict clean

in_progress.headline: The type layer is finished; the first real modules are next
in_progress.body:
The last run was the biggest so far — fourteen cycles, and it closed out three milestone tasks in a row.

The first nine cycles finished the shared type layer. Every section of the interface specification is now implemented as Pydantic models: agent runtime contracts, context bundles, the model and tool gateways, and the whole policy/approval/evaluation/memory/experiment family. Two import cycles surfaced along the way and were fixed the same way both times — pull the dependency-free type into its own leaf module that both sides can import.

Cycle ten added JSON Schema export for all 80 models, with a CI check that regenerates the document and fails the build if it differs from the committed copy. The last four cycles built the artifact content registry and its contract tests: for each artifact type, a real payload is wrapped exactly as a producer would wrap it, then recovered through the registry — proving the round-trip that the envelope's generic dict cannot enforce on its own.

With the schema work done, the next runs move to genuinely new ground: the policy rule set, the four MVP role specifications, and the Postgres schema for the event and artifact stores. Those three are independent of each other, and finishing any of them starts unlocking the M1 module work — the sequential prototype that has to produce one real end-to-end run.

recent_work.detail: All 11 registered artifact types now prove a real payload round-trips losslessly through the envelope.

recent_work.title: Artifact content-model registry
recent_work.detail: Maps each artifact type to the model that validates its content, so a producer can check before persisting.

recent_work.title: JSON Schema export for all shared types
recent_work.detail: One combined document for 80 models, regenerated and diffed in CI to catch drift.

recent_work.title: Experiment contracts complete the type layer
recent_work.detail: Finished the last interface section; a baseline arm is now structurally required in every experiment.

recent_work.title: Durable memory contracts
recent_work.detail: Agents can propose memory but never commit it — the curator field has no 'agent' member to select.
